## Controls

- [Controls](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/controls): Every visible thing on screen is a control. In Microsoft.UI.Reactor (Reactor) a control is the return value of a factory like TextBlock(...) or Button(...) — a plain element you compose, chain modifiers onto, and return from Render().
- [Forms and Input](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/controls/forms): Every form control in Reactor follows the controlled-input pattern: you own the value, you provide the change handler, and the control reflects your state. There is no two-way binding. The data always flows one direction.
- [Collections](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/controls/collections): When you need to render a list of data, Reactor provides three typed collection elements and a simple ForEach helper.
- [Text and Media](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/controls/text-and-media): This page covers display text, inline rich text, rich-text editing, and media controls in Reactor.
- [Status and Info](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/controls/status-and-info): Microsoft.UI.Reactor (Reactor)'s status and info controls report what the app is doing without stealing focus. Reach for them when the user needs to know something — a save succeeded, a long operation is running, a feature exists — and doesn't need to decide anything.
- [Dialogs and Flyouts](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/controls/dialogs-and-flyouts): ContentDialog, MenuFlyout, CommandBarFlyout and Popup: when to reach for each one, and how to drive them from component state.
- [Data System](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/controls/data-system): Reactor's data system provides a virtualized DataGrid<T> backed by a pluggable data source abstraction. You define columns (or auto-generate them), connect a data source, and the grid handles sorting, filtering, searching, selection, and inline editing.
- [Charting](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/controls/charting): ReactorD3 brings data visualization to Microsoft.UI.Reactor (Reactor). The chart DSL provides high-level LineChart, BarChart, AreaChart, and PieChart factories that produce standard Reactor elements. You bind data, configure appearance with a fluent API, and the chart renders as native WinUI shapes on a Canvas.
- [Win2D canvas](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/controls/win2d-canvas): Reactor.Advanced exposes the three Win2D canvas controls as Reactor elements. Add the package when you need immediate-mode drawing.

## Get started

- [Overview](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/get-started): Build native Windows apps with WinUI, in plain C#.
- [Installation](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/get-started/install): Set up your machine, create a Reactor project, and run it.
- [Your first app](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/get-started/first-app): Build a Reactor app step by step, from a single line of text to a working todo list.
- [Thinking in Reactor](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/get-started/thinking-in-reactor): Reactor asks you to think about UI in a new way. You don't create controls and then change them one property at a time. Instead, you write a function that describes what the screen should look like for the current state. When the state changes, Microsoft.UI.Reactor (Reactor) runs that function again and updates the real WinUI controls for you.
- [Coming from XAML](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/get-started/xaml-developers): If you know XAML, you already know most of Reactor. Reactor renders the same WinUI controls, with the same layout panels, theme resources and input events. What changes is how you describe them.
- [Samples](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/get-started/samples): The repository has more than 30 sample apps in its samples/ folder. Some are small and show one feature. Others are full apps with many components, real data and saved settings. Every sample is a normal .NET project that you start with dotnet run.
- [Cheat Sheet](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/get-started/cheat-sheet): Microsoft.UI.Reactor (Reactor) at a glance. Every row links to the page that covers it in depth.
- [Rules of Reactor](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/get-started/rules-of-reactor): Microsoft.UI.Reactor (Reactor)'s render loop has a small set of invariants. Most are enforced by analyzers, so a violation surfaces at build time with a specific code; the rest are conventions that the framework expects. This page lists them, names the analyzer where one exists, and shows the before/after pair so the catch is visible.

## Guides

### Core concepts

- [Components](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/components): Components are the building blocks of a Reactor app. Each component is a class with a Render() method that returns an element tree describing its UI.
- [Hooks](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/hooks): Hooks are functions you call inside Render() to manage state, side effects, and memoization. They replace the need for view models, event handlers, and lifecycle methods.
- [Effects and Lifecycle](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/effects): UseEffect runs side effects — code that reaches outside the component's render function. Timers, data fetching, subscriptions, and DOM manipulation all belong in effects, not in Render().
- [Context](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/context): Context lets you pass data through the component tree without threading it through every level of props. Define a Context<T>, provide a value at any level, and any descendant can read it with UseContext.
- [Commanding](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/commanding): A Command bundles an action with its metadata. Define it once and use it across buttons, menus, toolbars, and dialogs — the metadata stays consistent everywhere.
- [Advanced Patterns](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/advanced): Escape hatches for the few jobs the declarative model doesn't fit: error boundaries, memoized subtrees, element refs, direct property writes, view-model bridges, and custom hooks.

### Layout and styling

- [Layout](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/layout): Reactor provides a small set of layout primitives that compose to build any screen structure. Every layout element accepts children and optional spacing.
- [Flex Layout](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/flex-layout): FlexPanel is a Yoga-backed CSS Flexbox implementation, exposed through the FlexRow and FlexColumn factories. Reach for it when the layout needs alignment control, wrapping, or proportional sizing that VStack and HStack cannot express.
- [Styling and Theming](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/styling): Color and style your UI with theme tokens, named-style modifiers, and resource overrides that follow the Light, Dark, and high-contrast themes automatically.
- [Theming Tokens](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/theming-tokens): Reactor exposes 36 named theme tokens on the static Theme class plus a Theme.Ref(string) escape hatch for any XAML resource key.
- [Animation](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/animation): Reactor animations are declarative. You set the target value (opacity, scale, translation) and attach a transition modifier.
- [Input and gestures](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/input-and-gestures): Reactor's input surface is declarative: attach handlers via .On* modifiers and the reconciler wires WinUI events, auto-enables the matching flags (for example IsDoubleTapEnabled), and survives re-renders without re-subscribing the underlying WinUI event.

### Building apps

- [Navigation](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/navigation): Reactor uses a stack-based navigation model with type-safe routes. You define your routes as an enum, create a navigation handle with UseNavigation, and render the current page with NavigationHost.
- [Windows](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/windows): Most Microsoft.UI.Reactor (Reactor) apps start with the single window created by ReactorApp.Run. Larger desktop apps can open multiple native WinUI top-level windows with WindowSpec and ReactorApp.OpenWindow, while keeping the same declarative component model used inside a page.
- [Advanced Windowing](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/windowing-advanced): Some shell-window ideas are possible on Windows only by leaving the safe Reactor contract. We document the recipe so expert apps can make an informed choice, but Reactor does not ship these primitives as first-class WindowSpec fields.
- [Docking Windows](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/docking): Microsoft.UI.Reactor's docking system lets a single shell host multiple user-rearrangeable surfaces — the Visual Studio / VS Code / Photoshop / Figma layout idiom. Users drag tabs between groups, split panes, pin tool windows to a side, and tear panes out into floating sub-windows; layouts persist across sessions.
- [Desktop integration](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/desktop-integration): A desktop app does more than draw inside its windows. It can put an icon in the notification area, show progress on its taskbar button, offer shortcuts in a jump list, and start when the user opens a file or a link. It also shows the standard file dialogs and moves data through the clipboard and drag and drop.
- [Async Resources](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/async-resources): Microsoft.UI.Reactor (Reactor)'s async hooks — UseResource, UseInfiniteResource, and UseMutation — replace the "one UseState for data, one for loading, one for error, one UseEffect to tie them together" pattern. They own the fetch lifecycle: cancellation on deps-change, drop late results after unmount, shared caching across siblings, and stale-while-revalidate by default.
- [Persistence](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/persistence): UsePersisted holds a value past a component re-mount — the user navigates away, the component unmounts, the user navigates back, and the captured state is still there.
- [Services and dependency injection](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/services): Most apps have code that is not UI: a data store, a settings file, an HTTP client, a clock, a logger. Components need to reach that code, and tests need to replace it with fakes.

### Ship your app

- [Accessibility](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/accessibility): Reactor provides accessibility modifiers on every component. They map directly to WinUI's automation properties, so screen readers, keyboard navigation, and test tools work out of the box.
- [Localization](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/localization): Microsoft.UI.Reactor (Reactor)'s localization system wraps your component tree in a LocaleProvider that supplies an IntlAccessor to every descendant via context. You look up messages, format numbers and dates, and detect RTL layouts — all locale-aware, all reactive.
- [Testing](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/testing): Microsoft.UI.Reactor (Reactor)'s render loop is deterministic and synchronous. A Component mounted in a unit test renders, runs effects, accepts state updates, re-renders, and disposes through the same code path the WinUI host uses — minus the WinUI tree at the bottom.
- [Performance](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/performance): A top-down performance workflow: take a trace with dotnet-trace or PerfView, learn what each span means, find the outlier, and reproduce a benchmark so a regression has a number behind it.
- [Packaging](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/packaging): A Microsoft.UI.Reactor (Reactor) app is a normal WinUI / Windows App SDK executable — dotnet publish produces the deployable artifact and the framework itself adds nothing exotic to the project file.
- [Native AOT](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/native-aot): Native AOT compiles your app to native machine code when you publish it. The published app does not use a JIT compiler and does not load the .NET runtime host. Your code, Reactor and the .NET libraries you use become one native .exe.

### Recipes

- [Recipes](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/recipes): A recipe is a small composition of Microsoft.UI.Reactor (Reactor) primitives that solves a real UI problem — login, master-detail, settings, paginated list, modal confirmation, multi-step form, search-with-suggestions, command palette, drag-to-reorder. The recipes here are not exhaustive apps; each is a single screen showing the pattern, and each ships a tiny doc app you can clone and adapt.
- [Recipe: Command Palette](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/recipes/command-palette): A command palette is a filter-as-you-type list with a keyboard accelerator to open and Enter to execute. In Microsoft.UI.Reactor (Reactor) it's three UseState hooks, a static catalog of Command records, and an OnPreviewKeyDown handler — no menubar, no modal manager, no view model.
- [Recipe: Drag to Reorder](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/recipes/drag-reorder): Drag-reorder is a UseState<List<T>> plus a function that splices one item from one index to another. Microsoft.UI.Reactor (Reactor)'s keyed reconciler does the rest — moves preserve identity, so the same row element keeps its focus, its hover state, and its place in the visual tree. Pointer drag is one entry point; an Alt+Up / Alt+Down keyboard shortcut is the second, and it carries the accessibility story.
- [Recipe: Login](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/recipes/login): A Microsoft.UI.Reactor (Reactor) login form is four pieces working together: validated input, submit-gated state, an async call, and an error-display surface. The recipe below wires them with two UseState hooks and one UseMutation — no view model, no event handler classes, and no hand-rolled submitting / error flags.
- [Recipe: Master-detail](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/recipes/master-detail): Master-detail in Microsoft.UI.Reactor (Reactor) is the canonical multi-pane shape: a list of records on one side, the selected record's details on the other. The whole thing is one UseState for the selected id and two slots in an HStack.
- [Recipe: Modal dialog](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/recipes/modal-dialog): The modal is an element you return conditionally. There is no special "open dialog" API — when open is true the tree includes the modal panel layered over the page; when it's false the modal element is absent and the page renders alone.
- [Recipe: Multi-Step Form](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/recipes/multi-step-form): A wizard form is a step-index UseState plus a switch on which step renders. The field state lives in the same component as the step index, so moving forward and back never loses what the user typed — Microsoft.UI.Reactor (Reactor) doesn't unmount the surrounding component when the visible slot changes.
- [Recipe: Paginated List](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/recipes/paginated-list): A paginated list is four states sharing one source of truth: an initial load, a populated list, a "load the next page" affordance, and a terminal "no more results." UseInfiniteResource owns all four in Microsoft.UI.Reactor (Reactor) — the component below pattern-matches on LoadState and reads Items directly; there is no local UseState for loading or errors.
- [Recipe: Search with suggestions](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/recipes/search-with-suggestions): The pattern is two slots: an input that owns the query string, and a dropdown that shows zero or more suggestions filtered against a catalog. UseMemo keys the filter on the query, so a re-render that didn't touch the query is free — important for the keyboard-up- arrow-down-arrow loop where the suggestion index changes but the query doesn't.
- [Recipe: Settings page](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/recipes/settings-page): A settings page is many small persisted prefs side-by-side. Each preference is its own UsePersisted call with its own key — there's no central settings object that needs migration when one preference moves. The row layout is a single helper.

### Interop and migration

- [WinForms Interop](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/winforms-interop): Reactor components can run inside WinForms applications using XAML Islands. The Reactor.Interop.WinForms package provides XamlIslandControl — a standard WinForms control that hosts a Reactor component tree with full keyboard, accessibility, and theming support.
- [WPF Interop](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/wpf-interop): Host Reactor components inside a WPF app with a XAML island, until a first-class WPF host control ships.
- [Migration: Optional<T> controlled props](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/optional-t): Spec 050 changes controlled element-record properties from plain T to Optional<T>. Factory calls such as TextBox(text, setText), Slider(value, 0, 100, setValue), and ComboBox(items, index, setIndex) keep their existing plain-value signatures; they wrap the value in Optional<T>.Of(value) internally. Most app code therefore keeps compiling unchanged.
- [Migration: Windowing evolution](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/windowing-evolution): Spec 054 intentionally removes a few legacy windowing fields in favor of more explicit shapes. The new APIs are additive except for the breaking changes below.

## How it works

### Runtime

- [Architecture Overview](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/architecture-overview): This page maps Reactor's runtime end-to-end so the rest of the Under-the-hood track has a shared diagram to point at.
- [Reactivity Model](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/reactivity-model): This page is the why behind the hooks surface. If you've come from XAML and INotifyPropertyChanged, the change of model is larger than the syntax.
- [Hooks Internals](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/hooks-internals): One description of the storage shape behind every hook — enough to debug a HookOrderException, predict whether UseState returns a stable setter, and know when reaching for UseRef is correct.
- [Reconciliation](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/reconciliation): This page absorbs the legacy docs/reference/reconciliation.md. The goal is one place to learn how Reactor diffs trees — the same information, in the structure the rest of the guide uses, plus the source pointers that let you verify it.
- [Effects Scheduling](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/effects-scheduling): This page is about when UseEffect fires and why.
- [Threading and Dispatch](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/threading-and-dispatch): Microsoft.UI.Reactor (Reactor) has one UI thread invariant: the reconciler, every hook setter, and every WinUI property write must happen on the thread that captured the dispatcher at app bootstrap.
- [Element Pool](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/element-pool): The Microsoft.UI.Reactor (Reactor) element pool recycles unmounted WinUI controls so a scroll-heavy list or fast-mounting subtree doesn't allocate a fresh TextBlock / Button / Border on every render.

### Controls

- [The Control Reconciler Protocol](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/control-reconciler-protocol): This page documents the data path between the reconciler and the WinUI control it edits. It is for anyone extending Reactor with a new native control, or debugging why an existing element does not update the way it should.
- [Extending Reactor with Native Controls](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/extending-reactor-controls): How to wrap a native Windows control as a Reactor element — a third-party WinUI control, a custom Control subclass, or an existing WinUI control that the built-in catalog has not yet covered.
- [Modifier System](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/modifier-system): This page is the runtime view of the same fluent chain that Styling introduces from the surface.

### Input and motion

- [Animation Pipeline](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/animation-pipeline): This page maps the four authoring surfaces onto the underlying compositor and explains the trade-offs that pick one surface over another.
- [Focus and Input Internals](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/focus-and-input-internals): This page covers the input subsystem from the routed-event boundary through the Reactor hooks that observe it.

### Tooling

- [Source Mapping](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/source-mapping): "Source mapping" in Microsoft.UI.Reactor (Reactor) is the chain that ties a runtime artifact — an ETW event, a --preview overlay highlight, a thrown exception — back to the C# source that produced it.
- [Analyzer Architecture](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/analyzer-architecture): This page walks through the Reactor analyzer pipeline end-to-end: how a diagnostic descriptor wires into the C# compilation, what happens on each InvocationExpression, and how to add your own rule.
- [DevTools Internals](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/devtools-internals): This page covers the internals of Reactor's devtools — the MCP server that external agents talk to, the in-app dev menu, the runtime overlays, and the gate that keeps the whole subsystem out of retail.
- [Perf Instrumentation](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/perf-instrumentation): This page covers what Reactor publishes, where to read it, and how to get a clean trace.

## Tools

- [Developer tools](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools): Reactor comes with tools for the inner dev loop: the short cycle where you change code, see the result, and fix what is wrong. This page walks that loop one stage at a time. Each stage links to a page with the full details.

### Inner loop

- [Hot reload and live preview](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/hot-reload): Hot reload applies your code edits to a running app. You save a file, and the window updates in place. You keep the same process, the same window, and in most cases the same state. Reactor builds on .NET hot reload: dotnet watch sends the edit to the process, and Reactor re-renders every component against its existing hook state.
- [Devtools](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/devtools): Devtools let you look inside a running Reactor app and control it. They come in the Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Devtools NuGet package, and they only work in a build where you turn them on.
- [Visual Studio and VS Code extensions](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/vs-extension): Reactor has two editor extensions. Both are named Reactor Preview, and both show your running app next to the code.

### AI

- [Build with AI](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/build-with-ai): Reactor is a new framework, so AI models know little about it. Without help, an agent tends to invent API names or fall back to XAML, data binding, and view models. Reactor gives agents four kinds of help:

### Code quality

- [Analyzers](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/analyzers): Reactor ships a set of Roslyn analyzers that catch common mistakes while you write code: a hook inside an if, a list item with no key, a hard-coded color, an icon button with no name for screen readers. Each rule has an ID that starts with REACTOR. Many rules also have a code fix that rewrites the code for you.
- [mur CLI](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/mur-cli): mur is the Reactor command-line tool. It checks your code with fix hints, starts and drives devtools sessions, manages localization files, prints the API index for AI agents, and keeps a source checkout of Reactor up to date. Run mur --help to see the list of commands, and mur --version to see which version you have.
- [Diagnostics](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/diagnostics): This page shows how to read Reactor's diagnostics from a running app, including a Release build.

## Agent resources

- [llms-full.txt](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/llms-full.txt): The full Markdown of every page in one file.
- [Page Markdown](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/index.md): Append `.md` to any page URL to fetch that page as raw Markdown.
- [JSON API](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/api/docs/pages.json): Page index of the JSON docs API; each entry links the page's JSON and Markdown forms. Described by the OpenAPI document at https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/openapi.json.
- [Agent skills](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/.well-known/agent-skills/index.json): Agent Skills discovery index of the skills this site publishes.
- [API catalog](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/.well-known/api-catalog): RFC 9727 linkset of the APIs documented here.
- [AI catalog](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/.well-known/ai-catalog.json): ARD manifest of the agent-facing resources on this site (MCP server, skills, APIs).
- [agent-readability.json](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/agent-readability.json): Manifest of every agent-facing artifact on this site.
- [Sitemap](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/sitemap.xml): Every indexable page URL with its last-modified date.
